newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Old Middle East politics overtake new economics.
newsitem.headline: Old Middle East politics overtake new economics.

text.p: By now, according to the visionaries of the Oslo accords, the economies of the Middle East should be ringing to the sound of swords being beaten into ploughshares.
Instead the Israeli-Palestinian autonomy agreement, the cornerstone of a wider peace, is crumbling, sending foreign investors running for cover.
Israel, as the regional economic powerhouse, stood to gain most from the 1993 Oslo agreement.

But the crisis in talks on extending Palestinian self-rule since the election of Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing Likud government in May, culminating in unprecedented Israeli-Palestinian fighting last month, has clouded Israel's economic horizon, economists and market analysts say.
"Israel is no longer sexy," said Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg, head of securities marketing at Bank Hapoalim. "It could take quite a while to be sexy again," she told Reuters.

Foreign investors are sitting on their money, waiting to see if the climate of confidence created by the peace process can be salvaged, said Jonathan Kolber, head of Claridge Israel, a big investor in Israel, handling Charles Bronfman's portfolio.
The peace process was not the engine of Israel's economic rebound after the 1991 Gulf War but it brought the prospect of stability and expanding markets beloved of investors, economists said.

The assassination of Yitzhak Rabin a year ago gave peace a jolt but his successor as prime minister, Shimon Peres, forged ahead talking of a new Middle East with borders open to trade, and multi-billion-dollar infrastructure projects linking Israel by road, rail and pipeline to the Moslem world.
"Peres's vision of a new Middle East is not going to happen, it's just froth," said Pinchas Landau, an economic analyst and commentator.
"The economy was slowing down anyway. The violence has exacerbated this and recessionary forces have been strengthened," he said.
Economists have begun lowering their forecasts for Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth since the fighting last month in which 60 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died.
Baudet-Trajtenberg revised her forecast of 5.3 percent growth for 1996 and 3.6 percent for 1997 to five percent and 2.5 percent.
Assaf Rezin, a Tel Aviv University economics professor and adviser to the Israel Manufacturers Association, said growth could slow to two percent next year.
"Growth could slow to three to four percent this year, which is half of what it has been for the past six years, and to two to three percent next year," Rezin said.

Besides hitting foreign investment the unravelling of the peace process will harm tourism and distract Netanyahu from the economic overhaul he promised during his election campaign, economists and political analysts believe.

Economists expect total foreign investment, which leapt from $800 million in 1994 to $2.2 billion last year, to fall off next year. Investment in Israel's high-tech and software sector will not be so badly affected, they say, because most of those companies are export-oriented and quoted on NASDAQ in New York not on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.

But an illustration of the international climate came last week when plastics maker Plasson, the first Israeli company to seek a full listing on the London Stock Exchange, postponed the offering because of political tension.
The Tel Aviv stock market has dropped nearly 12 percent since Netanyahu took office in June.
Tourism, which flourished after Oslo, is likely to drop next year by 10 to 15 percent, according to Baudet-Trajtenberg, knocking one percentage point off GDP.

Economists doubted whether political tension would immediately harm immigration from the former Soviet Union, one of the motors of growth in the early 1990s. But a sustained economic slide could deter skilled workers from coming or staying.
Rezin believes lower growth will keep Israel's chronic current account balance of payments deficit high, and widen the budget deficit because of lower tax revenues.
The projected $4.9 billion current account shortfall for 1996, which represents between four and five percent of GDP, will remain as high or even grow next year, he said.

Economists said real estate prices in Israel could slide and long-term savings continue to erode. Exporters complain that the shekel is overvalued against the dollar, hampering their competitiveness, and ordinary Israelis wince at real interest rates of 6.5 percent.
This week Netanyahu locked horns over interest rates with the Bank of Israel, which wants to keep inflation, currently around 11 percent a year, in check.

Landau fears political turmoil could either blow the Netanyahu government off its reformist course or give it the pretext to shelve a painful overhaul. Netanyahu has said he wants to liberalise the economy, privatise industry and wean Israel off $1.2 billion a year in United States economic aid which free-marketeers say distorts the local economy.
"The real problem now is that the government's ability to address structural problems has been severely impaired," Landau said.
Immediately after the violence Kolber said Israel was at a crossroads and could go the way of either fragmented Bosnia or the post-War success story of Japan.
Since then the United States has stepped in to try to rescue the peace process.
Had this made Kolber change his mind?
"Absolutely not," he said.
